verses.1: Al-Mizan reads (98:1) as God’s enduring custom: people remain subject to divine guidance and clarification until a clear outward proof comes; only then, with no excuse left, are they released to choose, as in (9:115). ‘Those who disbelieved’ means those rejecters among—not all—the People of the Book and the polytheists; min is partitive, and the latter class comprises those other than the People of the Book. The future al-bayyinah, the manifest outer proof, is Muḥammad, his mission, message, or Qur’an. Al-Mizan identifies the proof further as Muḥammad reciting pure ṣuḥuf, the Qur’an’s revealed portions, untouched by falsehood, containing qayyimah writings: divine beliefs and ordinances that uphold human society’s well-being. It judges this reading consistent with the sūrah’s context despite extensive exegetical disagreement.

verses.4: Al-Mizan distinguishes this verse from (98:1): it concerns the People of the Book’s internal disagreements after their prior books and prophets had made the divine message clear, whereas the earlier verse concerns rejection of Muḥammad and his Book. It answers why the verse seems to single them out by taking ‘those who were given the Book’ as broader than the Qur’anic term ‘People of the Book.’ God gave every people a divine code to judge their disputes; once truth had removed their excuse, humanity fell into religious disagreement—some forgetting, distorting, preserving, or believing what it received. The phrase therefore includes polytheists as well as the People of the Book.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says the Messenger’s and the purified scripture’s command is to worship God sincerely as ḥunafāʾ, maintain prayer, and pay zakāt: the upright religion. Ḥunafāʾ, plural of ḥanīf, denotes turning from both excess and deficiency to the balanced middle; prayer and zakāt are singled out to stress worship directed exclusively to God and spending wealth for His sake. ‘The upright religion’ may mean the one religion carried by all revealed scriptures, not a new innovation, or the Qur’an’s upright ordinances that secure society’s well-being. In either sense it is divine monotheism, confirmed and guarded in the Qur’an, and promotes humanity’s true interests. Al-Mizan presents this as the sūrah’s proof of Muḥammad’s universal mission: God’s principle of completing proof applies to all; earlier peoples already received evidence and divided; therefore those called to this upright religion must believe and follow it.
verses.6: Al-Mizan says that after God’s custom of guidance sent clear evidence commanding the upright religion, those who rejected it are warned: the faithless among the People of the Book and the polytheists remain eternally in hell and are the worst of al-bariyyah, creatures.
verses.7: Al-Mizan contrasts the preceding verdict: believers who do righteous deeds are the best of creatures, just as evil was confined to the disbelievers.
verses.8: Al-Mizan explains ʿadn as stability and permanence, so the Gardens of Eden are everlasting, and remaining forever reinforces that meaning. God’s pleasure is an attribute of action, manifested in the reward granted for faith and righteous deeds. Fear of the Lord is the mark assuring eternal happiness: knowledge of God produces awe, which produces faith—acknowledging Him as Lord and object of worship—and righteous action.
